glossary.gloss: The port city of Athens, a few miles southwest of the city proper. Socrates and Glaucon have walked down to it for the new festival.
Plato's older brother and son of Ariston. He accompanies Socrates to the Piraeus and stays for the discussion.
The father of Glaucon (and of Plato). Mentioned only to identify Glaucon by lineage.
Here the Thracian goddess Bendis, identified with the Greek Artemis, in whose honor the new festival is held.
A Thracian moon-and-hunt goddess whose festival (the Bendidea) is being introduced at the Piraeus; the Greeks identified her with Artemis.
Of Thrace, the region northeast of Greece. The Thracian community in the Piraeus holds its own beautiful procession at the festival.
The Greek goddess of the hunt and the moon, here equated with the Thracian Bendis.
Son of Cephalus and brother of Lysias; he stops Socrates on the road and hosts the gathering, then takes over the argument about justice from his father.
The aged, wealthy father of Polemarchus in whose house the dialogue takes place. He opens the conversation with reflections on old age and wealth, then leaves to tend the sacrifices.
Another of Plato's brothers, Glaucon's brother, present at the festival and the discussion.
Son of the Athenian general Nicias; one of the young men at the gathering.
A prominent Athenian general, named here only as the father of Niceratus.
A brother of Polemarchus, found at the house; later a famous Athenian speechwriter.
Another brother of Polemarchus present at the house (not the sophist of the same name).
A sophist from Chalcedon who bursts into the debate to argue that justice is simply 'the interest of the stronger.' He is Socrates's chief opponent in Book I.
From Chalcedon, a Greek city on the Asian side of the Bosphorus; the epithet identifying Thrasymachus.
A man 'the Paeanian' (of the Athenian deme Paeania) present at the gathering; he takes no active part.
Belonging to Paeania, a district (deme) of Attica; the epithet of Charmantides.
Son of Aristonymus; a guest who briefly intervenes to defend Thrasymachus, arguing the 'stronger' means whatever the ruler thinks his interest is.
The father of Cleitophon, named only to identify him.
The philosopher who narrates the dialogue and leads the inquiry, questioning each speaker's definition of justice while professing to know nothing himself.
The great Athenian tragic poet, quoted by Cephalus: in old age he was glad to have escaped the 'mad master' of sexual desire.
The Athenian statesman, quoted as having told a man from Seriphos that fame depends partly on one's city, not merit alone.
A man from Seriphos, a small, obscure Aegean island; used by Themistocles as a byword for an insignificant place.
A citizen of Athens; in Themistocles's retort, being Athenian is part of what made him famous.
The father of Cephalus, who (Cephalus says) reduced the family fortune.
The celebrated Greek lyric poet, quoted by Cephalus on how 'sweet hope' is the kind nurse of the just man's old age.
An early Greek poet whose saying-that justice is repaying what is owed, giving each his due-Polemarchus defends and Socrates dismantles.
The epic poet, cited because he praises Autolycus for skill in theft, used to push the claim that the just man would also be a good thief.
The maternal grandfather of Odysseus in Homer, famous for excelling 'in theft and perjury.'
The Homeric hero; mentioned only as the grandson of the thief Autolycus.
One of the legendary Seven Sages of Greece, named among the wise men a true saying might be wrongly attributed to.
Another of the Seven Sages of Greece, likewise named as a wise man.
The tyrant of Corinth; Socrates suggests a rich, power-hungry ruler like him, not a sage, coined 'help friends, harm enemies.'
A king of Macedon, listed among powerful, wealthy men who might have authored the cynical view of justice.
The Persian king who invaded Greece, cited as an example of a mighty man confident in his own power.
A wealthy Theban politician, named as another rich and mighty man who might have coined the cynical maxim.
A famous pancratiast (all-in fighter/wrestler); Socrates uses him to mock Thrasymachus's definition-that the strong man's diet isn't therefore good for the weak.
A competitor in the pankration, the brutal Greek combat sport combining boxing and wrestling.
A professional teacher of rhetoric and argument who charged fees; the term carries a sense of cleverness for its own sake. Thrasymachus is the resident sophist here.

The central subject of Book I: what it is to be just-variously proposed as truth-telling and paying debts, helping friends and harming enemies, the interest of the stronger, and finally argued to be the excellence (virtue) of the soul.
Excellence-the quality that lets a thing do its proper work well. Socrates argues justice is the specific virtue (excellence) of the human soul.
Thrasymachus's bold definition: justice is nothing but whatever benefits those in power, since rulers make the laws to serve themselves.
The inner self that lives, governs, and deliberates. Socrates argues the soul has a proper function and a proper excellence (justice), so a just soul lives well and is happy.
Used here in the older sense of a thing's purpose or proper function-what it alone can do or do best (the 'end' of the eye is sight, of the soul, to govern and live).
A craft or skill (Greek techne)-medicine, navigation, music. Socrates argues every genuine art aims at the good of its subject, not the practitioner's own gain.
Farming; the cultivation of crops, given as an example of an art that produces a particular good (corn).
A herdsman who tends cattle ('neat' = cattle), paired with the shepherd in Thrasymachus's image of rulers fattening their 'flock' for their own profit.
A board game (checkers); used as an example where the skilled player, not the just man, is the better partner.
A curved cutting tool for trimming vines, used as the example of a tool whose proper 'end' is best fulfilled by the vine-dresser's art.
A worker who tends and prunes grapevines; the craftsman whose art the pruning-hook properly serves.
In this period, one who brings malicious legal accusations to trap people with their own words; Thrasymachus accuses Socrates of arguing 'like an informer.'
A person devoted to fine food; Socrates compares himself to one who snatches a taste of every dish without finishing any-jumping from topic to topic.
Petty thieves who cut purses to steal; Thrasymachus distinguishes such small-time criminals from the grand, admired injustice of the tyrant.
Kidnappers who seize people (often to enslave them); listed among the criminals punished for small-scale wrongdoing.
An old, polite way of saying 'please' or 'I pray you'; Socrates uses it to coax Thrasymachus to share his view.
An old word for 'no,' often used to correct or push back-'Nay, Socrates; the doctrine is immoral.'
Archaic 'you' (singular), as in Socrates's mock-grand address: 'O thou heir of the argument.'
Archaic for 'from which it follows' or 'from where'-'whence follows that justice is the injury... of the stronger.'
Here meaning non-sacred or secular-the tyrant seizes things 'sacred as well as profane.'
Internal strife or rebellion; injustice is said to breed sedition that makes any group incapable of united action.
Deep ill-will or wickedness; Socrates offers it as a name for injustice, but Thrasymachus rejects it, calling injustice 'discretion' (good sense) instead.
Prudent good judgment; Thrasymachus provocatively names injustice 'discretion,' praising it as shrewd rather than vicious.
Greed for money or gain; named (with ambition) as something good men consider a disgrace, so they will not rule for pay.
People who work only for wages; good men avoid ruling openly for money lest they earn this name.
Self-control and moderation-one of the cardinal virtues. Raised as part of the inquiry into virtue and the well-ordered soul.
A poetic phrase (Homeric) for the edge or onset of old age; Socrates quotes it in asking Cephalus what late life is like.
The underworld, the realm of the dead, where (the old tales say) wrongs done in life are punished-a fear that grows on Cephalus as death nears.

A legendary Lydian shepherd who found a magic ring of invisibility and used it to seduce the queen, kill the king, and seize the throne. Glaucon uses him to argue that anyone able to act unjustly without being caught would do so.
The famously rich king of Lydia; mentioned here only as the descendant of Gyges, to date the legend.
An ancient kingdom in Asia Minor (modern western Turkey), the setting of the Gyges story.
The great Athenian tragic poet, quoted here both for the line about wishing 'to be and not to seem' good, and for verses that wrongly make the gods the cause of human guilt and ruin.

An early Greek poet (author of Works and Days and Theogony), cited as an authority who promised earthly rewards to the just and an easy road to vice, and who told the offensive tales of Uranus and Cronus.
A legendary early poet and seer, said to be a son of the Moon and the Muses, who (with his son) promised the just an afterlife of perpetual feasting and drunkenness.
The legendary musician-poet, named with Musaeus as author of the ritual books that promised expiation of sins through sacrifices and ceremonies.
An early Greek poet, mockingly called 'greatest of sages' for the image of the crafty fox-advice to hide one's true nature behind a show of virtue.
A city near Athens; site of a battle where Glaucon and Adeimantus distinguished themselves, commemorated in the elegiac verses Socrates quotes.
The primal sky-god of Greek myth; Hesiod's tale of how his son Cronus mutilated and overthrew him is condemned by Socrates as a 'bad lie' unfit for children.
Son of Uranus who overthrew his father and was in turn overthrown by his own son Zeus; his violent myth is one Socrates would ban from the city.
The chief Greek god. Socrates objects to poems showing him dispensing good and evil from two casks, sending lying dreams, or instigating strife-since God must be good and truthful.
The smith-god; Socrates rejects the Homeric tale of Zeus hurling him from heaven for defending his mother Here, as an unacceptable story of divine family violence.
The queen of the gods (Hera), wife of Zeus; cited in two banned tales-being bound by Hephaestus and being beaten, and disguising herself as a begging priestess.
The goddess Athena; named among the gods wrongly blamed by poets for human wrongdoing-here for the breaking of oaths and treaties.
A goddess of divine law and order, named (with Zeus) as wrongly said to have stirred up strife among the gods.
A Trojan archer in the Iliad who broke the truce by wounding Menelaus; Socrates objects to poets blaming the gods for this act that was really Pandarus's own.
A sea-god famous for changing shape; Socrates says God should not be slandered as a shape-shifter like him, since the divine is unchanging.
A sea-goddess, mother of Achilles; cited for the tale that Apollo sang of her son's blessed future at her wedding and then killed him-an unacceptable picture of a lying god.
The god of prophecy and song; in the Aeschylus passage he is said to have prophesied a long, healthy life for Thetis's son and then slain him, which Socrates condemns as making God a deceiver.
The Greek commander at Troy; Socrates refuses to admire the Homeric episode in which Zeus sends him a deliberately lying dream.
A mythical mother whose children were killed by the gods as punishment for her pride; her sufferings are cited as a tragic subject poets must not blame on a good God.
A figure of myth whose 'house' (descendants) was famous for a chain of crimes and disasters; named as a tragic subject that must not be attributed to God's malice.
A river-god of Argos; named in a quoted line about Here disguised as a priestess begging alms 'for the life-giving daughters of Inachus.'
A city-state in the Greek Peloponnese, named in the quoted line about the river Inachus.
The Greek deities collectively. A central concern of Book II is how the gods should be portrayed: as wholly good, truthful, and unchanging-never as the cause of evil, deceivers, or shape-shifters.
The Greek underworld of the dead; mentioned for the punishments poets imagine there, such as the wicked carrying water in a sieve.

Glaucon's opening framework: goods wanted only for themselves, goods wanted both for themselves and their results, and goods wanted only for their results. He asks where justice belongs; Socrates puts it in the highest class.

The popular view Glaucon revives: justice is not a real good but a compromise. Since doing wrong unpunished is best and suffering wrong is worst, people agree by law and covenant to avoid the worst; justice is merely the lesser evil people tolerate.

Glaucon's thought experiment: a ring that makes its wearer invisible. He argues that with such power both the just and unjust man would act unjustly, proving people are just only because they fear getting caught.

glossary.term: to be and not to seem
glossary.gloss: The ideal of the truly just man, drawn from Aeschylus: he wants really to be good, not merely to appear good. Glaucon's challenge strips away reputation to test justice for its own sake.
Socrates's method of founding an imaginary State 'in idea' so that justice, hard to see in one person, can be read in larger letters in a whole community.
The founding principle of Socrates's city: each person should do the single job they are naturally fitted for, since work is done better and more plentifully when one person practises one craft.

Glaucon's expansion of the simple 'true and healthy' city into one with sofas, dainties, perfumes, and luxuries-a 'State at fever-heat' whose unlimited wants lead to seizing neighbours' land and to war.
The class of soldier-protectors Socrates introduces to defend the enlarged city. War is itself a specialized art, so guarding requires people of special nature, fully trained for it and nothing else.

The fierce, courageous, fearless quality of soul (thumos) that makes a creature ready to fight. The guardian must have it-yet also be gentle to friends-just as a good watchdog is both fierce to strangers and gentle to its own household.

The two halves of the guardians' traditional education: 'gymnastic' (physical training for the body) and 'music' (here meaning literature, story, and the arts for the soul). Education begins with music, including the tales told to children.

Socrates's proposal that the founders set up a 'censorship of the writers of fiction,' approving good tales and rejecting bad ones, because the stories children first hear shape their characters permanently.

Socrates's idea of the lie everyone genuinely hates: not a falsehood spoken in words, but real ignorance lodged in the soul about the highest things-'the lie in the soul'-as opposed to the merely useful spoken lie.

Wandering begging-priests and soothsayers who, Adeimantus complains, go to rich men's doors promising to absolve sins through sacrifices, charms, and incantations-exploiting the idea that the gods can be bribed.

Secret religious rites and initiations (here associated with Musaeus and Orpheus) said to redeem people from punishment after death-criticized as encouraging the belief that wrongdoing can be ritually washed away.
The goddesses of poetry and the arts; named as the mothers (with the Moon) of Musaeus and Orpheus.
Referred to as a divine parent: Musaeus and Orpheus are called 'children of the Moon and the Muses.'

Pertaining to Eleusis and its famous mystery cult; Socrates jokes that the few who hear the forbidden myth of Cronus should sacrifice not a cheap '(Eleusinian) pig' but a huge, unobtainable victim-so few would qualify to hear it.
Eager to fight or argue; combative. Glaucon is called 'the most pugnacious of men.'
To contradict or deny. Used in the sense of speaking against or disputing a claim.
To what place; where to. Socrates says to watch 'whither desire will lead them.'
The setting or bezel of a ring that holds the stone or seal. Gyges turns the 'collet' of the ring inward to become invisible.
Made of brass or bronze. Gyges sees a 'hollow brazen horse' inside the chasm.
A deserved reward or recompense. Endless drunkenness is mocked as 'the highest meed of virtue.'
People who deliver formal speeches of high praise. The 'panegyrists of justice' praise it only for its rewards.
Perhaps; possibly. Used in the sense of 'unless by chance there be some one...'
To grant or bestow, especially as a favor. Musaeus and his son 'vouchsafe' grand gifts to the just.
A swamp, bog, or pit of mud. The wicked are imagined buried in a 'slough in Hades.'
Workers who dress and finish tanned leather. Listed among the trades the city requires.
Lady's maids who attend to dressing and hair. Listed among the servants of the luxurious city.
Professional reciters of epic poetry, especially Homer. Listed among the entertainers of the luxurious city.
High-class kept women or paid female companions. Listed among the luxuries of the fevered city.
A farmer; one who works the land. The first and most basic worker in Socrates's city.
A digging tool like a pickaxe, used in farming. Cited as a tool the farmer cannot also make himself.
Shopkeepers who buy and sell goods within the city marketplace, as distinct from 'merchants' who travel between cities.
A well-ordered State or political community. Used for the just city being founded.
Executed by being thrust through with a stake-a gruesome death. Glaucon imagines the falsely-accused just man finally 'impaled.'
Whipped or flogged as punishment. Part of the torment Glaucon imagines for the just man thought unjust.
Lines written in iambic meter, the standard meter of Greek tragic dialogue. Referenced for the tragedy about Niobe.
Verses in elegiac couplets, a poetic form used for commemoration; the form of the lines praising Glaucon and Adeimantus after the battle of Megara.
Ritual offerings of liquid (such as wine) poured out to the gods. Cited in the Homeric line about how the gods may be appeased.
Acts performed to make amends for sin or guilt, such as sacrifices and atonements. Criticized as the false belief that wrongdoing can be bought off.
Another name for the god of the underworld and ruler of the dead.
The blind prophet of Greek myth who, in Homer, keeps his power of mind even among the dead while other souls are mere flitting shades.
The queen of the underworld, wife of the death-god; in the cited verse she alone grants the dead Tiresias the gift of keeping his mind.
A river of the underworld whose name ('river of wailing') evokes horror; Plato lists it among the dreadful names of the world below that should be dropped.
The chief river of the underworld, its name a byword for the terrors of death; Plato wants such fear-inducing names banished from the guardians' poetry.
The bodiless, ghostly souls of the dead as imagined in the underworld. Here 'sapless shades' and 'flitting shades' name the feeble phantoms of Homer's afterlife.
Loud expression of grief; weeping and wailing for the dead. Plato wants poets to stop showing famous men and gods given over to it.
A song or strain of mourning for the dead. Plato rejects the mournful 'strains of sorrow' and weepings he discusses.
The greatest Greek warrior at Troy, son of the goddess Thetis and the mortal Peleus. Plato objects to Homer's portrait of him weeping, raging, and acting greedily, as a bad model for the young.
The aged king of Troy. Plato dislikes Homer's image of him rolling in the dirt and begging during the war, as unworthy of imitation.
A son of Zeus and ally of Troy, killed by Patroclus; in the cited line Zeus laments his fated death.
Achilles' closest companion at Troy, killed by Hector. He also appears tending wounds, as the friend treating injured warriors.
The father of Patroclus; 'Patroclus the son of Menoetius.'
A leading Greek warrior at Troy, cited approvingly for the line urging a comrade to sit still and obey orders.
The god of war, caught by Hephaestus in an adulterous tryst with Aphrodite; Plato rejects such tales of the gods.
The goddess of love and desire, caught with Ares in Hephaestus's trap; Plato treats the story as an unworthy depiction of the gods.
Self-controlled and moderate, especially in pleasures of the body. Plato makes temperance a chief virtue the guardians must learn.
The old tutor of Achilles, who advised him to accept gifts before helping the Greeks; Plato faults this counsel as teaching greed.
The greatest Trojan warrior, killed by Achilles, whose body Achilles drags around Patroclus's tomb. Plato refuses to believe Achilles ransomed the corpse only for payment.
An epithet of Apollo meaning 'the one who shoots arrows from afar,' referring to the god as a deadly archer.
A river-god to whom Achilles had vowed his hair; Plato lists Achilles' impieties toward such divinities among the tales to reject.
The wise centaur who tutored Achilles (and other heroes); Plato calls Achilles 'the wise Cheiron's pupil.'
The mortal father of Achilles, described as 'the gentlest of men and third in descent from Zeus.'
The Athenian hero, called son of Poseidon, blamed (with Peirithous) for a 'horrid rape'; Plato rejects such tales of heroes as sons of gods.
The god of the sea, named here as the divine father of the hero Theseus.
A hero called son of Zeus who, with Theseus, set out to commit a notorious abduction; Plato refuses to credit such stories.
The mountain near Troy where, in the cited verse, the ancestral altar of Zeus stands; a sacred high place of the gods' supposed kin.

In Plato's analysis of style, telling a story by taking on a character's voice and manner (as in drama), as opposed to plain narration in the poet's own person. The actor or poet who does this is an imitator.
Telling a story straight, in the poet's own voice without impersonating the characters, as opposed to imitation/drama. Plato favors it (with little imitation) for the guardians.
The priest of Apollo at the opening of the Iliad who begs Agamemnon to release his captive daughter; Plato uses these lines to illustrate narration versus imitation.
The father of Agamemnon and Menelaus; 'the two sons of Atreus' are the leading Greek chiefs.
One of Homer's names for the Greeks who besieged Troy. Same people as the 'Greeks' elsewhere.
The island home of Odysseus; named as one of the settings of Homer's narrative in the Odyssey.
A type of Greek choral hymn (originally to Dionysus) in which the poet speaks throughout in his own person; Plato gives it as the best example of pure, unimitative narration.
The all-imitating, show-everything theatrical style that mimics any character or sound; Plato calls it popular but unfit for the guardians' single-minded city.
A juror or judge in an Athenian law court. Plato's example of how each man in the ideal city does one job only: the farmer is not also a dicast.
A fragrant resin used as perfume and in ritual; Plato pictures anointing the all-imitating poet with it before honorably sending him away.
The Greek musical modes or scale-types, each thought to express a particular mood or character. Plato keeps only the warlike and the temperate modes and banishes the mournful and soft ones.
A Greek musical mode; in its 'mixed/tenor' and 'full-toned/bass' forms it expresses sorrow, and (relaxed) it is a soft drinking mode. Plato banishes it as mournful or enervating.
A Greek musical mode classed as 'soft' or 'relaxed' and fit for drinking; Plato rejects it as useless for warriors.
A Greek musical mode Plato keeps: the firm, warlike strain that fits a brave man facing danger and hardship with steady resolve.
A Greek musical mode Plato keeps: the strain of peace, persuasion, and temperate, moderate action.
Using every mode and scale at once; the elaborate, many-noted music Plato rejects in favor of a few simple modes. Also applied by analogy to over-rich cooking.
A small stringed instrument plucked to accompany song; one of the few instruments Plato allows in the city, associated with Apollo.
A wind instrument (the Greek aulos) capable of many modes at once; Plato bans it as the worst for encouraging complex, indulgent music.
A satyr of myth famous for the flute (aulos), who lost a music contest to Apollo. Plato sides with Apollo's lyre over 'Marsyas and his instruments.'
A mild Socratic oath, roughly 'I swear,' sworn by the dog (associated with the Egyptian dog-headed god Anubis); a characteristic way Socrates avoids swearing by the gods.
A noted Athenian music theorist and teacher; Plato defers to him to explain which rhythms express which characters.
A type of poetic rhythm (a metrical foot) mentioned among those Damon analyzed.
A poetic rhythm based on the dactyl (one long plus two short beats), also called 'heroic' because it is the meter of epic; one of the rhythms discussed.
A poetic rhythm built on the iamb (a short beat followed by a long one); one of the meters Damon classified.
A poetic rhythm built on the trochee (a long beat followed by a short one); paired with the iambic in Damon's analysis.
A group of four notes (a four-note scale segment) that is the basic building block of Greek musical scales.
The virtue of a free, generous, gentlemanly character; one of the essential forms the guardians must learn to recognize, opposite of meanness.
Greatness or nobility of soul and bearing; one of the virtuous 'forms' the well-educated guardian must come to know.

Physical training and athletics; for Plato the partner of music in education. He argues its real aim is to shape the soul, not just the body, and that it should be simple and military, not the regimen of professional athletes.
The narrow strait (the modern Dardanelles) by which the Greek army camped at Troy; Plato notes Homer's heroes ate no fish though they were on its shores.
Of Syracuse in Sicily, a city famous for rich, elaborate cooking; Plato uses 'Syracusan dinners' as an example of indulgent eating to avoid.
Of Sicily, proverbial for fancy cookery; 'the refinements of Sicilian cookery' stand for unhealthy luxury in diet.
A courtesan from Corinth, a city notorious for prostitution; Plato lists keeping one as a luxury the warrior in training must give up.
Athens-style sweets and pastries; cited as another self-indulgent delicacy unfit for the guardians' simple diet.

The god/hero of healing, son of Apollo, ancestor of physicians. Plato praises his old, no-nonsense medicine that cured definite ailments and let hopeless or idle patients go, rather than coddling the chronically sick.
The healer-heroes descended from Asclepius (Machaon and Podalirius) who served as physicians at Troy; models of the brisk, practical medicine Plato admires.
A Greek hero wounded at Troy who, in Homer, is given a strong drink (Pramnian wine with barley and cheese) to heal him; Plato's evidence that old medicine was simple.
A strong, dark Greek wine; in Homer it is mixed with barley-meal and cheese into a restorative drink for wounded heroes.
A thick drink of wine (or milk) mixed with other ingredients; here the Pramnian-wine-and-barley draught given to wounded soldiers.
A trainer of sickly constitution who, Plato says, invented 'valetudinarian' medicine-prolonging a miserable, ailing life by constant self-treatment.
A chronic invalid obsessed with his own health, forever nursing his ailments; Plato's term for the lingering, self-coddling life Herodicus pioneered.
King of Sparta, Helen's husband and brother of Agamemnon; wounded by Pandarus and healed by the sons of Asclepius.
The legendary king whose touch turned things to gold; 'as rich as Midas' is a byword for immense wealth.
The writers of tragic drama; Plato blames them, along with Pindar, for impious tales such as the bribing of Asclepius.
An early Greek gnomic poet quoted for the maxim that as soon as a man has a livelihood he should practise virtue.
A flexible willow twig used for binding; 'bending like a withy' describes the litigious man twisting and wriggling out of justice.
Plato's name for the warrior class who enforce the rulers' decisions-the soldier-helpers under the ruling guardians. In the metals myth they are the men of silver.
The ruling-and-protecting class of the ideal city. In the strictest sense the word names the wise rulers who guard the state; the soldier-helpers under them are the auxiliaries.
The energetic, courageous, fiery part of human nature-the source of courage and anger-that gymnastic is meant to train and music to temper. Plato pairs it with the philosophical (gentle) part.

The kind of made-up foundational story Plato proposes as the 'noble lie': an old Phoenician-style legend (Phoenicians being proverbial inventors of clever fictions) to bind the citizens to their city.

Plato's famous 'noble lie'-a single grand falsehood, fed first to rulers then to all, to make citizens love their city: the myth that they were born from the earth and that God mixed different metals into their souls.
Born from the ground itself; in the noble lie the citizens are told they were formed in the womb of the earth, their common mother, making them all brothers.
The core of the noble lie: God mingled gold in the rulers, silver in the auxiliaries, and brass and iron in the farmers and craftsmen, so that rank should follow the metal in one's soul.
Stubbornly disobedient, resisting control; describing any within the city who might rebel and need to be suppressed.
Burial; honorable interment. The successful guardian is to be rewarded with sepulture and other honors at death.
Calm, even-tempered composure; the good man bears misfortune 'with the greatest equanimity' instead of lamenting.
Soft, unmanly, weakened-used of nerves or character made overdelicate. Plato fears frightening tales and soft music make the guardians effeminate.
Outstanding courage and skill, especially in battle; the Greeks 'marched breathing prowess.'
The art of medicine, or medicine itself as treatment; Plato mocks the man who must 'go abroad for his law and physic.'
To that place; toward there. 'Whither the argument may blow, thither we go'-wherever it leads, there we follow.
The sanctuary of Apollo regarded as the religious center of the Greek world, the 'navel of the earth' where the god is said to sit and interpret religion to all mankind.

An Athenian in a story Socrates tells: walking up from the harbor he both longed to look at executed corpses and was disgusted with himself for wanting to-an example of anger taking the side of reason against desire.
The father of Leontius in the anecdote Socrates relates; mentioned only as 'Leontius, the son of Aglaion.'
The Greeks' own name for themselves; Socrates says no rival state its equal will be found 'either among Hellenes or barbarians.'
Here simply non-Greeks, all peoples who were not Hellenes-without the modern insult; used to mean 'foreigners' generally.
A people of the region north of Greece (Thrace), cited as an example of a nation marked by 'spirit' or high temper, to show that a trait in a state comes from its individuals.
A nomadic people of the northern steppes, named alongside the Thracians as 'northern nations' famous for spirited, fierce temperament.
A trading and seafaring people of the eastern Mediterranean, cited (with the Egyptians) as exemplifying the love of money.
The people of Egypt, named with the Phoenicians as an example of a nation characterized by love of money.

The book's founding principle that the city is built for the greatest happiness of the entire state, not the disproportionate happiness of any one class; each class gets the share of happiness its nature allows.
Named as the two corrupting enemies of the crafts and the city: wealth breeds luxury and idleness, poverty breeds meanness and bad work, and both breed discontent.
An idiom for the money and resources needed to wage war; Adeimantus worries the moneyless city will lack them against a rich enemy.

glossary.term: the right size of the city
glossary.gloss: Socrates' rule that the state should grow only as far as it can while still remaining one and self-sufficing-neither large nor small, but unified.
The four excellences the perfect state must have-wisdom, courage, temperance, and justice; Socrates locates each one in the city in turn.
Here, good counsel-the knowledge that deliberates about the whole state and its dealings with others; it resides in the small ruling class of true guardians.
Defined as a kind of salvation: the soldier class's steadfast holding-on, in pleasure and pain, to the law-instilled belief about what truly should and should not be feared.
Socrates' formula for justice-each person practicing the one task he is naturally fit for and not being a busybody in others' work; its opposite, meddling between classes, is injustice.

glossary.term: the three parts of the soul
glossary.gloss: Socrates' division of the soul into three: the rational part (reason), the spirited part (passion/anger), and the appetitive part (desire); they parallel the rulers, auxiliaries, and producers of the state.
The reasoning part of the soul-the part that reflects on better and worse and ought to rule and care for the whole soul, matched to the city's ruling guardians.
The desiring part of the soul-the irrational element that hungers, thirsts, and craves bodily pleasure and gain; the largest and most insatiable part, matched to the producing class.
The spirited part of the soul-the seat of anger, indignation, and high temper; when well brought up it is reason's natural ally against the appetites, like a guard dog obeying the shepherd.

glossary.term: the parallel of soul and State
glossary.gloss: The method of reading justice 'writ large' in the city first, then finding the same three-part structure and the same justice in the individual soul.
Socrates' musical image for the just soul: reason, spirit, and appetite bound together like the high, low, and middle notes of a scale into one well-tuned, self-mastered nature.

glossary.term: virtue is the health of the soul
glossary.gloss: The closing analogy: virtue is the natural good order of the soul's parts (like health in the body) and vice is their disorder (like disease)-so justice is worth having for its own sake.
An old word for 'to this place; here'; in 'Come up hither' it means 'come up here.'
An old phrase meaning 'and similar things; and the rest of that kind'-e.g. 'markets, police, harbours, and the like.'
The introduction or opening preamble of a speech; Glaucon complains he is growing impatient at the length of Socrates' long lead-in.
A quack remedy or dubious cure-all; the foolish invalids keep hoping to be cured by whatever nostrum anyone recommends.
Burning a wound or tissue (with a hot iron) as a medical treatment; listed among the cures that will not help the patient who refuses to change his ways.
Chasing after women; given as one of the indulgences the stubborn invalid must give up-'eating and drinking and wenching and idling.'
The marketplace and public square of a Greek city, the center of commerce and civic life; Socrates dismisses the need to legislate in detail about its everyday dealings.
An ancient unit of length, roughly the forearm (about 18 inches); used in the gibe that a crowd of bad measurers might declare a man 'four cubits high.'
A many-headed monster of Greek myth that grew two heads for each one cut off; an image for futile petty reforms that only multiply the troubles they try to remove.
The prized, costly purple dye of antiquity (Tyrian purple); used in the analogy about preparing white wool so the dye holds fast-as good education fixes the 'dye' of law in the soul.

Strong alkaline washing solutions (like a harsh detergent); in the dye image, even the most powerful lyes cannot wash out a properly fixed color, as pleasure and fear cannot wash a well-trained courage out of the soul.
An old adjective for the desiring, appetite-driven part of the soul-the seat of bodily cravings and greed for gain; the largest part, needing to be ruled by reason.

The two names Socrates gives the good constitution he has described-rule by one outstanding man (monarchy) or by several (aristocracy); he treats them as a single form since the trained rulers keep the same laws either way.
The center of the world, identified with Delphi; Apollo is described as the god who sits there interpreting religion to all mankind.
A vote or expression of support; Adeimantus offers to 'add my suffrage'-that is, his endorsement-to Damon's and Socrates' view.
In feudal terms, a subordinate bound to obey his lord; used in the image of injustice as a rebellious subject rising up against the rightful prince he is naturally bound to serve.
The crime of violating something sacred, such as robbing a temple; named among the wrongs the just man will never commit.
Being 'master of oneself': the well-ordered soul in which the better, rational part rules the worse, appetitive part; the essence of temperance.
The Greek goddess of divine retribution against arrogance; Socrates prays she won't punish him for the bold claims he is about to make.
A reference to the legend of the poet Arion, who was saved from drowning by a dolphin; Socrates jokes that some such miraculous rescue may save him in this difficult argument.
The oracle of Apollo at Delphi; here the marriage of certain brothers and sisters would be permitted only if it received this oracle's sanction.
A great warrior of the Trojan War in Homer's poems, mentioned as having been honored with choice cuts of meat after distinguishing himself in battle.
Greece, the homeland of the Hellenes, regarded as a single people united by blood and friendship.
The people of Crete, named as among the first Greeks to introduce the custom of exercising naked.
The Spartans; named here as adopting, after the Cretans, the custom of nude athletic exercise.
A wrestling-school or exercise ground in ancient Greece, where athletes trained naked. Socrates imagines women exercising there alongside men.
Public grounds for athletic training and exercise in ancient Greece (the plural of gymnasium).
Literally 'lover of wisdom'; defined here as one who loves all knowledge and can grasp truth and absolute beauty itself, not merely beautiful things-and who alone is fit to rule.
The love and pursuit of wisdom and truth; the book argues that until political power and philosophy are united in the same people, states will never be free of evils.
Socrates' famous claim: cities will have no rest from evil until kings become philosophers or philosophers become kings-political power and wisdom united in the same person.
Another name for true philosophers-those who love truth itself in every thing, as opposed to 'lovers of opinion' who chase appearances.
People who delight in beautiful colors, shapes, and tones but cannot grasp absolute beauty itself; Socrates says they have opinion, not knowledge, and are not real philosophers.
True understanding, which Socrates says is directed at being-what truly and unchangeably is-and is infallible, unlike opinion.
A faculty between knowledge and ignorance; it is directed at things that both are and are not (the shifting world of appearances) and can err, unlike knowledge.
That which truly and fully is-the real, eternal, unchanging reality that is the object of genuine knowledge.
Pure non-existence or nothingness; the absolute negation of being, of which there can be no knowledge or even opinion.
Beauty itself-the single, unchanging Form of the beautiful, as opposed to the many particular beautiful things; only the philosopher can grasp it.
Here a technical term for the Form-the one unchanging reality (such as beauty or justice itself) that particular things merely share in or imitate.
A power in us by which we do what we do-such as sight, hearing, knowledge, or opinion; each faculty is defined by its own object and result.
The contrast between a single unchanging Form (e.g., beauty itself, which is one) and the countless particular things that share its name and appear in many lights.
Pertaining to marriage or a wedding (from Hymen, the Greek god of marriage); here the staged marriage festivals at which guardians are paired.
A rigged lottery that the rulers will secretly arrange so that pairings appear to be decided by chance, letting the less worthy blame bad luck rather than the rulers.
Plato's proposal that among the guardians no one has a private spouse or child; wives, husbands, and children are held in common, and no parent knows his own child.
Strife within a single people or city-internal, domestic conflict, distinguished here from 'war,' which is conflict with foreigners.
Winners of the ancient Olympic games, considered supremely happy and honored; the guardians' blessed life is said to be even greater than theirs.
Festivals honoring Dionysus, the god of wine and theater, featuring dramatic and choral performances; the music-lovers chase from one to the next to hear every chorus.
Gladly; with pleasure or willingness. Socrates says he 'would fain have uttered' the thought-would have been glad to say it.
Truly; indeed. An emphatic old-fashioned way of affirming something.
Abbreviation of 'namely' or 'that is to say,' used to introduce a specific point being spelled out.
Cuts of meat along the backbone of an animal; 'long chines' were the choice portions awarded to Ajax as an honor.
Meanness, stinginess, or pettiness unworthy of a free and noble person; here applied to robbing the bodies of the dead.
To raze-to tear down or destroy completely (here, houses). An older spelling of 'raze.'
Stripping the dead of armor and possessions as spoils of war; the book condemns this practice as cowardly and greedy.
Supreme; of the greatest importance. The management of family life is said to have a 'paramount influence' on the state.
Lack of moral or sexual restraint; disorderly indulgence, which the rulers forbid in the ideal city.
Marriage as an institution; here it is to be made 'sacred in the highest degree' through regulated festivals.
Accidental, unintended killing of a person-held here to be a lesser crime than deceiving people about beauty, goodness, or justice.
Complete and perfect; of the highest skill. The rulers will need 'consummate skill' to breed the guardians well.
A form of government or political constitution; the overall ordering of the state.
A skilled manual craftsman, such as a potter or shoemaker; one of the ordinary working classes of the state.
A man whose chronic ill health kept him out of politics and so, by accident, left him free for philosophy—Socrates' example of a 'bridle' that holds someone back from public life.
An early Greek philosopher; cited here for his saying that the sun is snuffed out every evening and rekindled every morning.
The supreme object of knowledge in Plato's scheme—the source that makes everything else knowable and worth having; Socrates calls it the highest of all studies.
The eternal, unchanging realities (e.g. absolute beauty, absolute justice) that lie behind the many changing things we see; they are 'known but not seen.'
The lover of truth and of eternal being; here defined by a cluster of traits (truthfulness, good memory, proportion, temperance) and argued to be the only fit ruler.
Socrates' parable of a ship whose ignorant sailors mutiny against the true navigator—an image of why the genuine philosopher is shut out of politics.
Socrates' comparison: just as the sun lets the eye see visible things, the idea of good lets the mind know the realm of truth, while being the source of being itself.
Socrates' image of a line cut into unequal parts to map four levels of awareness—from shadows and images up through belief, mathematical reasoning, and pure dialectic.
aliases: take a line which has been cut into two unequal parts

glossary.gloss: The highest method of reasoning, which rises from assumptions all the way to the first principle and moves through pure ideas alone, without relying on the senses.
Starting assumptions taken for granted (as geometers assume the odd, the even, and figures); dialectic treats them only as stepping-stones, not as final truths.
The realm of things we perceive with the senses—copies and appearances—contrasted with the intelligible world grasped by the mind.
The realm of unchanging realities grasped by thought rather than sight; the higher of the two worlds in the divided line.
The world of things that come to be and pass away—the shifting realm that yields only opinion, not knowledge.
Paid teachers of rhetoric and argument; Socrates redefines the term to mock them, calling the opinionated public itself the greatest Sophist.
Socrates' image of the Sophist as a keeper who learns to handle a huge animal—the crowd—calling its likes 'good' and dislikes 'evil' without knowing real right and wrong.
The mass of ordinary people guided by appearances and popular opinion—incapable, Socrates says, of being philosophers.
Devoted followers or worshippers; here, those dedicated to philosophy.
Greedy for possessions and gain; the true philosopher, absorbed in the soul's pleasures, is the opposite.
The legal stripping of a person's rights and property, often as punishment; named alongside confiscation and death as the public's coercive weapons.
The seizing of a person's property by authority—one of the penalties the crowd uses to force its will.
Imprisonment or confinement; Socrates pictures an unworthy man who has 'just got out of durance' rushing into philosophy.
A lowly traveling mender of pots and pans; used as an image of a base craftsman who presumes to take up philosophy.
A maker or craftsman; used both for nature as 'the artificer of the senses' and for the philosopher as an 'artificer of justice.'
A flowing-out or emanation; the eye's power to see is described as an effluence dispensed from the sun.
Clever but hollow arguments meant to deceive—the kind of plausible-sounding falsehoods produced by unworthy students of philosophy.
An idle, empty talker; one of the contemptuous names the mutinous sailors give the true navigator.
A mocking term for someone with his head in the clouds; here flung at the true pilot (and philosopher) who studies the stars and sky.
Socrates' famous private 'divine sign' (daimonion)—an inner voice or monitor that warned him away from certain actions; he notes how rare such a thing is.
A personification of philosophy as a presiding goddess; Socrates says the ideal State will exist 'whenever the Muse of Philosophy is queen.'
Mental and intellectual training, contrasted with physical exercise—the inner discipline that should grow as the mind matures.
Despises or scorns; said of the lofty soul who looks down on the corrupt politics of his city.
The fire used to purify gold; an image for the testing by which the truest, most patriotic candidate is proved fit to rule.
aliases: gold tried in the refiner's fire

glossary.gloss: The true nature or being of a thing—what each thing really is, grasped as a single 'idea'; the good is said to exceed even essence in dignity and power.

Plato's famous image: prisoners chained in an underground den see only shadows on a wall and mistake them for reality. It pictures how most people live among illusions until education turns the soul toward the truth.
aliases: prison-house is the world of sight

glossary.gloss: The chained people in the cave who can see only shadows. They stand for ordinary human beings who take the appearances around them for the whole of reality.
The flickering images the prisoners see cast on the cave wall, which they mistake for real things. Here they symbolize the false impressions and mere opinions people accept instead of truth.

The fire burning behind the prisoners whose light throws the shadows on the wall. In the allegory it stands for the visible sun and the world of the senses, a lesser source of light than the true Good.
The painful climb of the freed prisoner up out of the cave into the sunlight. It represents the soul's upward journey from the world of appearances to true knowledge and the Good.
The highest object of knowledge, which Plato says appears last and only with great effort. It is the source of truth and reason and the cause of everything beautiful and right, symbolized by the sun.

In the allegory, the real sun the freed prisoner finally sees, which gives life and seasons to the visible world. It stands for the idea of the Good, source of all light and truth in the intellectual world.
The trained philosopher who is compelled to return to the cave and govern. Plato argues the best rulers are those reluctant to rule, who care for truth and justice rather than power.
The study of pure number, which Plato makes the first science of the rulers' higher education. It draws the soul away from the senses toward abstract truth, useful both in war and in philosophy.
The science of figures and space, the second branch of the rulers' study. Plato values it not for practical surveying but because, rightly pursued, it turns the mind toward eternal truth.

The study of the heavens, made the fourth science. Plato wants it pursued through mathematical problems rather than mere stargazing, so it lifts the soul toward true being rather than fixing it on visible motions.
The mathematical study of musical harmony, treated as the sister science of astronomy. Plato faults those who only measure heard sounds and praises seeking the natural harmonies of number itself.
Plato's image for the mind's inner faculty of insight, more precious than ten thousand bodily eyes. Education does not put sight into it but turns it from darkness toward the light of truth.
A clever Greek hero of the Trojan War, in tragedy credited with inventing number and counting the ships. Socrates cites him to argue that even a general needs arithmetic.
The legendary master craftsman and artist of Greek myth. Socrates uses him as the type of a great artist whose beautiful works are still only visible images, not eternal truth.
The famous early Athenian lawgiver and sage. Socrates says Solon was mistaken to claim an old man can keep learning many things, since youth is the time for hard study.
Followers of Pythagoras who studied numbers, music, and the heavens as kindred sciences. Plato agrees with them that astronomy and harmonics are sisters but faults them for stopping at heard sounds.
The city besieged by the Greeks in the Trojan War, where Agamemnon led the army and Palamedes is said to have numbered the ships.

In Greek myth, a paradise where heroes dwell after death. Plato uses it both for philosophers who selfishly want to stay in contemplation and as the final reward of the rulers who have served the State.
Beings ranked between gods and mortals, often deified heroes. Plato proposes the State honor its greatest dead rulers as demigods, or at least as blessed and divine.
In the older Greek sense, training in poetry, song, and harmony that shaped character through rhythm and tune. Plato says it made the guardians harmonious but gave them no real science.
A person who argues to win or for amusement rather than to find truth, contradicting and refuting for sport. Plato warns young students of dialectic against becoming eristics.
In Plato's fourfold scheme, the kind of thought used in mathematics, clearer than mere opinion but below true science or knowledge, because it leaves its assumptions unexamined.
The realm grasped by the mind rather than the senses, the world of eternal being and the Forms, opposed to the visible world.
To congratulate, or to count oneself fortunate. The freed prisoner would felicitate himself, that is, count himself lucky, on his escape from the cave.
A blissful sight of the highest reality. Plato uses it for the philosopher's contemplation of the Good, which makes him unwilling to come back down to ordinary human affairs.
Freed from a false belief or error. The prisoner is disabused, that is, corrected, when he is released and shown that the shadows were not real.
A devoted follower or worshipper of something. Plato speaks of the votaries of the sciences and the true votary of philosophy who must be wholehearted, not half-idle.
Lame or crippled. Plato calls a soul "halt and lame" when it is uneven in virtue, for example loving truth only halfheartedly.
The topmost stone that finishes and crowns a wall or arch. Plato calls dialectic the coping-stone of the sciences, the crowning study above all the rest.
An introductory piece before the main performance. Plato calls all the mathematical sciences merely the prelude to the real strain, which is dialectic.
A melody or tune, here used as a metaphor (playing on a Greek word meaning both "law" and "song"). The "chief strain" is dialectic, the true music the soul must learn after its prelude.
A final settling or release, here meaning death or final end. The man who never grasps the Good arrives at the world below and has his "final quietus."
A small pick used to pluck the strings of a lyre or similar instrument. Socrates mocks the harmony-teachers with talk of the blows the plectrum gives the strings.
Falsely substituted or not genuine. Plato imagines a "supposititious son" raised believing his foster parents are his real ones, as a parallel for the student who loses faith in inherited values.
The lawgiver who founds and orders the State. Plato reminds Glaucon that the legislator aims at the happiness of the whole city, not of any one class.
A turning-around of the whole soul from the world of becoming toward true being. For Plato, education is this conversion, not the pouring of knowledge into an empty mind.

A government ruled by honor and ambition, where the love of victory and glory dominates rather than wisdom or wealth. It is modeled on the warlike Spartan state and is the first stage of decline from the ideal city.
A government in which the rich hold power based on a property qualification, and the poor are excluded. Plato describes it as a city split into two hostile camps of rich and poor.

A government born when the poor overthrow the rich, granting everyone equal freedom and choosing officials by lot. Plato pictures it as colorful and free but disorderly, treating all desires and people as equal.

The worst form of government, where a single ruler seizes absolute power, usually emerging from democracy when a popular protector turns predator. Plato calls it the harshest slavery, born from excessive freedom.
Literally 'rule of the best' — Plato's ideal government led by philosopher-kings and guardians, from which all the lesser forms decline. The just and good man corresponds to it.
A Greek island whose constitution, like Sparta's, was admired for its discipline and military training. Plato cites it as a real example of the honor-loving timocratic state.
The militaristic Greek city-state famous for valuing honor, war, and austere discipline over wealth and philosophy. Plato uses it as the model for timocracy.
An Athenian tragic poet whom Socrates calls great but criticizes for flattering tyrants, quoting his line 'Tyrants are wise by living with the wise.'
A river in Lydia (in Asia Minor) referenced in the oracle given to Croesus. The phrase pictures a coward fleeing along its pebbly banks.

Zeus as worshipped at an ancient Arcadian shrine where, by legend, anyone who tasted human flesh mixed into the sacrifice was turned into a wolf. Socrates uses the tale as an image of how a popular protector becomes a tyrant.
Of Arcadia, a rugged inland region of the Peloponnese in Greece. The reference is to the Arcadian shrine of Lycaean Zeus and its werewolf legend.

In Homer's Odyssey, a people whose lotus fruit made visitors forget home and abandon all purpose. Plato uses 'returns into the country of the lotus-eaters' to mean surrendering to idle, dissolute pleasures.

The stingless male honeybee that does no work and lives off the hive — Plato's image for the idle spendthrift who consumes without producing. Some drones are harmless paupers, others 'have stings' and become criminals.
A heavily armed Greek foot soldier who fought in close formation. Listed among the productive civic roles the impoverished man can no longer fill.
The raised speaker's platform in the Athenian assembly. Plato says the drones 'keep buzzing about the bema,' dominating public debate.
A resident foreigner living in a Greek city without full citizenship. Plato notes that in extreme democracy the metic becomes treated as the equal of the citizen.
Greedy for wealth; miserly. Plato applies it to the oligarchical man, who is single-minded in his hunger to accumulate money.
Stingy and excessively thrifty, spending as little as possible. It describes the oligarchical man's grudging, miserly way of life.
A person who wastes money recklessly. Plato uses it both for the ruined oligarchic youth and for the idle wastrels who help bring on democracy.
Farmers; those who till the soil. Listed among the many trades one overburdened oligarchic citizen is forced to combine.
One who murders or assaults his own father or close kin. Plato applies it to the tyrant who turns violently on the people who created him, 'his father.'
A curved Eastern sword, here part of the royal regalia (with tiara and chain) Plato pictures adorning the enthroned love of money in the oligarch's soul.
An ornate Eastern royal headdress signifying kingship. Plato uses it to dress up the greedy appetite that the oligarchical man crowns as ruler of his soul.
People who accuse others before the courts, often falsely and for gain. Plato cites them as how the timocratic father is ruined and how tyrants destroy enemies.
Thieves who slit purses to steal money — pickpockets. Listed among the criminals who lurk wherever there are paupers.
Wrongdoers or criminals. Plato groups them with thieves and temple-robbers as the human 'stinging drones' found near poverty.
Unrestrained indulgence in pleasure without moral limits. Plato uses it for the life into which the democratic man falls, free of the discipline he was raised under.
Two of the four bodily humors of ancient medicine, thought to cause disease when out of balance. Plato compares the idle drones to phlegm and bile that sicken the body of the state.
Stripped of property and civil rights, usually by a legal condemnation. Plato says the tyrant funds himself from the confiscated fortunes of 'attainted persons.'
The armed personal escort a rising tyrant demands from the people for his 'protection.' Plato identifies this famous request as the decisive step into open tyranny.

The worst type of person in Plato's scheme: someone ruled by lawless desires with a 'master passion' (love/lust) as tyrant of his soul, who tramples law, family, and shame. The book argues he is the most miserable of all men.
Belonging to democracy. Here used of the 'democratic man,' the type from whom the tyrannical man develops—a person who indulges all his desires more or less equally without a guiding principle.

Bodily cravings and desires—for food, drink, sex, money, and pleasure. Plato sorts them into necessary, unnecessary, and unlawful, and treats the appetitive part as the lowest of the soul's three parts.
Outside the restraint of law, reason, and shame. The 'lawless' desires are the wild, criminal cravings that surface in dreams in everyone but rule the waking life of the tyrannical man.
Desires so forbidden that decent people suppress them—the wild urges that, Plato says, emerge in sleep when reason is unconscious and which the tyrant indulges while awake.
The rational, calculating, truth-seeking part of the soul—the highest of the three parts, which ought to rule. Also called the principle of knowledge or the lover of wisdom.
The passionate, ambitious part of the soul—the seat of anger, courage, and the love of honor and victory. The middle of the soul's three parts, ideally reason's ally.
Reason in its noblest function—the part of the soul that contemplates truth and ought to govern the lower desires. Plato also calls it the higher element.
Plato's division of the soul into three parts—reason (the rational), spirit (the passionate), and appetite (the desiring/money-loving). Justice is each part doing its own work under reason's rule.

The distinct pleasures corresponding to the soul's three parts: the pleasure of knowing the truth, of honor and victory, and of gain or bodily satisfaction. One is genuine and the other two are 'spurious.'
One of the three classes of men, ruled by the spirited part and driven to win fame, victory, and distinction. Also called the contentious or ambitious type.
One of the three classes of men, ruled by appetite and devoted to money and material pleasure. Also called the money-maker or money-lover.

Plato's image of the appetitive part of the soul: a beast with a ring of heads of all kinds of tame and wild animals that it can grow and change at will. Justice means taming it; injustice means feeding it.
Plato's image of the spirited part of the soul—the bold, fierce element of courage, anger, and pride. The just person makes it an ally; pride and bad temper come from letting it grow too strong.
Plato's image of reason as a small inner human being inside the composite soul-creature. The just person gives this inner man mastery over the lion and the many-headed beast.

A monstrous beast of Greek myth combining parts of different animals (lion, goat, serpent). Plato cites it as an example of a single creature made of many natures, like his composite image of the soul.
A sea-monster of Greek myth, a many-natured creature with a ring of dogs' heads around her waist. Plato lists her among the mythic composite beasts that model his many-headed image of the soul.
The many-headed dog of Greek myth that guards the underworld. Plato names him as an example of an ancient mythological creature combining several natures into one.
Zeus in his role as deliverer and protector. The traditional 'third libation' was poured to Zeus the Savior, so Socrates invokes him for the decisive third proof of the just life's superiority.

An early Greek lyric poet who told the story that the real Helen never went to Troy—the Greeks and Trojans fought only over a phantom 'shadow' of her. Plato cites this to compare false pleasures to a deceiving image.
Helen of Troy, whose abduction sparked the Trojan War. Plato alludes to the legend that the Greeks fought only over a phantom image of her—an emblem of chasing illusions instead of truth.
A woman of Greek myth who, bribed with a golden necklace, betrayed her husband Amphiaraus to his death. Plato uses her as the type of someone who sells what is most precious for money.
Literally Glaucon (and Plato), son of Ariston; the name Ariston puns on the Greek for 'best.' Socrates uses it to 'proclaim' that the best and justest man is also the happiest.
Relating to timocracy, the honor-loving form of government and character ranked second-best. One of the five types Glaucon scores from happiest to most miserable.
Relating to oligarchy, rule by the wealthy few, and the money-loving character it produces. One of the five constitutions ranked in the book's contest of happiness.
A base, despicable, cowardly wretch. Plato uses it for the man who would sell his own divine soul for money.
Excessive, fawning flattery. The real tyrant, Plato says, is forced into the greatest adulation and servility toward the worst of men.
Slavish, cringing submissiveness. Plato says the tyrant, though seemingly a master, is really a slave reduced to servility.
Emptiness; a state of being unfilled or depleted. Plato calls hunger and thirst 'inanitions' of the body, and ignorance and folly 'inanitions' of the soul.
The state of being fully satisfied or filled. Plato says the inexperienced mistake mere relief from pain for true satiety and pleasure.
Lacking moral restraint, especially sexually; dissolute and unrestrained. Used of the refined but wanton company that draws the young man toward excess.
Undisciplined, reckless, given to indulgence and lust. Describes the loose ways the future democrat falls into.
Loose in morals; debauched and self-indulgent. Plato pictures the tyrant's lusts let loose amid 'all the pleasures of a dissolute life.'
High-class prostitutes or paid female companions. Listed among the feasts, carousals, and revels that fill the tyrannical man's life.
Noisy drinking-parties and merrymaking. Part of the riotous life Plato ascribes to the tyrannical man.
Sexual relations between close relatives. Cited as one of the unnatural acts the wild beast within is willing to commit when reason sleeps.
Robbers who attack travelers on foot on the roads; muggers. Listed among the petty criminals the tyrannical types become.
A biting fly that torments cattle; figuratively, a relentless goad. Plato says a 'gadfly' goads the tyrant's soul so it can never rest.
A pang of conscience or guilt about doing wrong. Plato asks whether the tyrannical son would feel any compunction at tyrannizing over his own parents.
To adjust, moderate, or bring into proper balance. Plato says the wise man trains his body so as to 'attemper' it and preserve the harmony of the soul.
That which never changes—the immortal, eternal reality (the Forms), as opposed to the variable and mortal. Plato says it has the purest being and gives the truest knowledge and pleasure.

The number by which Plato calculates the king to live more pleasantly than the tyrant—three cubed (the tyrant being 'thrice removed' from true pleasure), raised to a solid. He notes it nearly equals the days and nights in a year.

glossary.term: a pattern laid up in heaven
glossary.gloss: Plato's image of the ideal city existing only as a model in heaven—a paradigm the wise person can look to in order to 'set his own house in order,' whether or not it ever exists on earth.
aliases: city which exists in idea only

glossary.gloss: The divine element within a person—reason or the soul's highest part. Plato says the noble subjects the beast to 'the god in man,' and that one should be ruled by 'divine wisdom dwelling within.'
Poetry that dramatically represents or impersonates people and actions (epic and tragedy), as opposed to hymns and praise-songs. Socrates argues it should be banned from the ideal State.
Socrates' charge against the artist: God makes the real Form, the carpenter makes a copy of it, and the painter or poet copies that copy — so the imitator's work stands three steps away from reality.
aliases: third in the descent from nature

glossary.gloss: How things merely look from a given angle, as opposed to what they truly are. Painting imitates appearance, not reality, which is why Socrates calls it deceptive.
Formal speeches or writings of high praise. Socrates says the true maker would rather be the subject of praise than the author of it.
A poetic meter used especially in the dialogue of Greek tragedy. Socrates lumps poets who write in it among the imitators.
The dactylic hexameter meter of epic poetry, as in Homer. Named 'heroic' because it told of heroes.
The musical ornaments of poetry — its measured beat, tuneful sound, and cadence. Socrates says these dress up the poet's ignorant words and make them seem wise.
Socrates' phrase for sweet, pleasure-giving poetry whose charm seduces a State away from law and reason.

glossary.term: ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry
glossary.gloss: The long-standing rivalry Socrates invokes between the philosopher's pursuit of truth and the poet's appeal to feeling and pleasure. He sides with philosophy.
The calculating, reasoning part of the soul that measures, judges, and trusts truth. Socrates says poetry bypasses it and feeds the lower, irrational part instead.
The lower, emotional part of the soul — the part that laments, lusts, and rages. Socrates says imitative poetry indulges and strengthens it at reason's expense.
An inflammation or disease of the eyes. Socrates uses it as an example of an evil natural to a thing — each thing has its own corrupting disease.
A fungus that spoils crops; given as the characteristic 'evil' or rot of corn.
Socrates' argument that the soul cannot be destroyed: since not even its own evil (injustice) kills it, nothing can, so it must live forever.
In this book, the immortal, divine part of a person — proven deathless and shown to be best off when it follows wisdom and justice.
A sea-god whose true form is hidden under encrustations of shells, seaweed, and stones from the waves. Socrates uses him as an image of the soul disfigured by its life in the body.
A legendary ring of invisibility (from earlier in the Republic) that lets its wearer do wrong undetected. Socrates says the truly just man would act justly even with it.
A mythical cap of invisibility worn by the god of the underworld. Like the ring of Gyges, it stands for the power to do wrong unseen.
A count of twenty. 'Three score years and ten' means seventy years — the proverbial span of a human life.
The hero of Socrates' closing myth: a slain warrior, son of Armenius, who revives on his funeral pyre and reports what he saw of the soul's fate in the afterlife.
The father of Er, the warrior whose vision of the afterlife closes the Republic.
A native of Pamphylia, a region in southern Asia Minor. Er is described as 'a Pamphylian by birth.'
A pyre — the heap of wood on which a dead body is burned. Er revived as he lay upon his.
In the Myth of Er, the resting-place between heaven and earth where souls gather after judgment to rest, talk, and await their next journey.
A tyrant who, a thousand years before Er, murdered his father and brother. In the myth he is one of the incurable sinners seized at the cavern's mouth and never allowed to leave the underworld.
The great cosmic shaft, turning on the knees of the goddess Necessity, around which the whole heaven and all the planetary circles revolve.
The goddess on whose knees the cosmic spindle turns and whose daughters are the three Fates. She personifies the binding order of the universe.
The weighted disk on a spindle that keeps it spinning. In Er's vision the heavens are made of eight nested whorls, one inside another, each a planetary sphere.
An ancient Greek warship rowed by three banks of oars. Its 'under-girders' (the cables bracing the hull) are Socrates' image for the band of light holding the universe together.
In the myth, one of eight singing spirits, each riding a circle of the spindle and sounding a single note; together their voices make the harmony of the cosmos.
The three daughters of Necessity who sing of past, present, and future and turn the cosmic spindle: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos.
One of the three Fates; she sings of the past and dispenses the lots and sample lives from which the souls choose their next existence.
One of the three Fates; she sings of the present and, with her right hand, turns the outer circle of the spindle to ratify each soul's chosen destiny.
One of the three Fates; she sings of the future and spins each soul's thread of life to make its choice irreversible.
Wreaths or garlands worn on the head. The three Fates wear them in their white robes.
In the Myth of Er, the guardian spirit or personal destiny that each soul chooses for its next life and that watches over and fulfills that choice.
The central moment of Er's myth: each soul, by lot, must pick its next life from many samples. Souls are responsible for their choice — 'God is justified.'
Unbreakable, hard as diamond or steel. Socrates says one must carry into the next world an 'adamantine faith in truth and right.'
In the myth, the barren, treeless waste the souls cross before reincarnation, on the way to the river of forgetting.
The river (also called the river of Forgetfulness, the Lethe) from which every soul must drink before rebirth; its water erases all memory of the other world.
The Phaeacian king to whom Odysseus told his wandering-tales in the Odyssey. Socrates contrasts his own myth with 'the tales which Odysseus tells to the hero Alcinous.'
A mythical bard who challenged the Muses in song. In the myth his soul chooses the life of a nightingale.
The father of the warrior Ajax.
A famous swift huntress of myth. In Er's vision her soul, drawn by an athlete's glory, chooses the life of a male athlete.
The builder of the Trojan Horse (son of Panopeus). His soul chooses to be reborn as a woman skilled in crafts.
The ugly, foul-mouthed jester of the Iliad. Among the last to choose, his soul takes the form of a monkey (an ape).
Another name for Sparta, cited for its good order under the laws of Lycurgus — an example of real legislation Homer never matched.
The legendary lawgiver who gave Sparta its constitution. Socrates names him as a true benefactor of his city, unlike the poets.
An ancient lawgiver of the Greek cities of Italy and Sicily, named as a real legislator who actually improved his State.
Thales of Miletus, an early philosopher and inventor, cited as a man of real practical wisdom Homer never equaled.
A Scythian sage famed for clever inventions, named as another practical genius unlike the merely imitative Homer.
The philosopher and teacher whose devoted followers preserved a whole 'Pythagorean' way of life — proof, Socrates argues, of real wisdom, which Homer left no such following to show.
A companion of Homer whose name (suggesting 'child of flesh') Socrates mocks; tradition said he neglected Homer in the poet's own lifetime.
A famous traveling sophist and teacher. Socrates cites him as someone beloved for his teaching, by contrast with the neglected Homer.
Another celebrated sophist and teacher, named alongside Protagoras as a teacher whose pupils prized him.
The person who lives by justice. The whole book builds to showing that he is best off — rewarded by gods and men in this life and in the afterlife.
The branch or wreath awarded to a winner. Socrates uses it figuratively for the rewards the gods grant the just.
To loathe or detest utterly. Socrates says we praise in poetry the very grief we would 'abominate' in ourselves.
Haughtily disdainful or scornful. Used of the spectator who fears he'd seem snobbish if he refused poetry's emotional pleasures.
Inclined to laughter; relating to the urge to laugh. Comedy stimulates the 'risible faculty.'
